newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Danes set to veto EU stand on U.S. anti-Cuba law.
newsitem.headline: Danes set to veto EU stand on U.S. anti-Cuba law.

text.p: European Union diplomats said Sunday that they saw little hope of persuading Denmark not to veto a proposal for a united EU stand against Washington's controversial anti-Cuba trade law, the Helms-Burton Act.

EU officials said they were resigned to a Danish veto at a meeting of the bloc's foreign ministers in Luxembourg Monday, despite diplomatic efforts by the EU's executive, the European Commission, and its current president, Ireland.
"We have not given up hope but, given the strength of Copenhagen's convictions, it is hard to foresee a change of heart," said one senior diplomat.

Denmark stunned its EU partners last week by saying concerns over national sovereignty would prevent it approving laws to counter the Helms-Burton Act, an amalgamation of years of anti-Cuba policy that seeks to punish companies that make use of appropriated U.S. property in Cuba.
The Danish government is currently embroiled in a court case brought by a citizens' group that accuses it of handing too much sovereignty to the EU.

Copenhagen says it cannot go along with EU action based on a catch-all clause in the EU's founding treaties, which is regarded with suspicion by governments wary of ceding too much authority to the bloc.

Diplomats will instead concentrate their efforts on fine-tuning blocking tactics -- particularly one section which would allow the EU to waive an obligation for European companies or individuals not to comply with the act.
Nevertheless, one diplomat said having a proposal that couldn't be passed into law would be "like having a nuclear deterrent made out of cardboard."
The Danish decision will not affect a case brought by the Commission against the United States at the World Trade Organisation in Geneva.
A WTO panel is due to convene in November to rule on EU complaints that the act -- and similar laws that seek to quash trade with Iran and Libya -- is extra-territorial.

The EU foreign ministers meetingn Monday were due to discuss proposals that would allow countersuits to be brought anywhere in Europe against litigants who sue European companies or individuals for contravening the Helms-Burton Act.

Among other things, the act allows naturalised Americans, such as native Cubans, to take action in U.S. courts against foreign companies or individuals accused of gaining from investments made in property confiscated in Cuba since the 1959 Communist revolution.

The practical implications of the act have been suspended until January, ostensibly to give U.S. special envoy Stuart Eizenstat the opportunity to encourage Washington's allies to join efforts to isolate Havana but also to postpone the issue until after the presidential election Nov. 5.

Although President Clinton is known to privately oppose parts of the act, he was pressured into signing it into law in March after Cuba shot down two private U.S. light aircraft it said had strayed into Cuban airspace.
Following outrage from the EU, Mexico and Canada, Clinton suspended part of the act, although he passed another section that bars executives of "traffickers" from entering the United States.

Executives from Canadian mining conglomerate Sherritt International, among them EU nationals, have been barred from entering the United States. Washington is expected to name more companies it accuses of trafficking later this year.
The European Union is still studying proposals to bar U.S executives involved in litigation from the 15-nation bloc and has already begun compiling a "watchlist" of potential litigants.
